guide.title: Powderhouse Hill: South Berwick's town-owned rope tow, running since 1939
guide.intro: The town of South Berwick owns Powderhouse Hill; it is operated by the Powderhouse Hill Ski Club, reported by Seacoastonline as roughly 30 member families with Dan Boyle as club president at the time of that January 29, 2025 report, while a separate group, Friends of Powderhouse Hill, runs the concession stand under the umbrella of SoBo Central. Per the same article, the hill operates "Wednesday and Friday evenings as well as Saturday and Sunday afternoons, when snow allows," with the Marshwood high school ski team using it on other nights; rope tow tickets were priced at $5 at the time of that report. Per New England Lost Ski Areas Project (NELSAP), the hill sits "on Agamenticus Road where it intersects with Route 4 in South Berwick, Maine," and the Powderhouse Hill Ski Club was, per Maine state incorporation records cited by that source, "incorporated December 14, 1964."

sections.heading: A snow-dependent season, and a name from gunpowder
sections.body: By the time of the January 29, 2025 Seacoastonline article, the hill had already opened five times during the 2024-25 season — "five times as often as all of last year" — after a snowstorm the week before left the snowpack cold enough that, per the club, "none of the snow melted after the storm." A club representative described the decision: "When we made the decision to open (last) Monday after the storm, we looked and said it's marginal but it's better than not skiing." Club president Dan Boyle credited the town directly in the same article: "We owe the town a huge amount, they have really improved the hill through the draining plans." Per NELSAP, the hill's name comes from its history with gunpowder; early settlers Thomas and Elizabeth Butler owned the property beginning in 1698, and William Hardy built the first rope tow on the slope "about 1939" — NELSAP's own word, repeated three times on the page — when the hill was owned by Herbie Day.

sections.heading: Town ownership, and a groomer the source calls uncertain
sections.body: Per NELSAP, the town purchased the property in the early 1990s, and "the club and town work in harmony to keep the hill open for the public to enjoy." NELSAP presents two accounts of the tow's power history that the source itself flags as disagreeing: a club history book describes founder William Hardy's original Model A truck engine being replaced in the 1970s by an unnamed air-cooled four-cylinder engine, while separate contributors' recollections instead describe a 1938 Ford V8 truck whose original engine was replaced by a 37 HP air-cooled Wisconsin engine during the club's 1960s era. Either way, per NELSAP, the engine turns "a hard rubber, grooved drive wheel off the truck rear end," powering an 800-foot rope tow from a base with "a small lodge...with a snack bar and wood stove." In 2008 the club built a "drag type" snow groomer pulled behind a snowmobile — "to our knowledge," per NELSAP's own hedge, the first time the hill has been consistently groomed since its inception. Per the same source, the hill connects to hiking trails across South Berwick Water District land toward Berwick Academy, which "has used the convenient loop for cross-country training," and a Girl Scout-established geocaching site sits at the hill's top.

sections.heading: In South Berwick
sections.body: The Sarah Orne Jewett House, per Wikipedia's article on the house, is "a two-story wood-frame structure with clapboard siding," built in 1774 for merchant John Haggins, combining Georgian architecture with Greek Revival elements; it is stewarded by Historic New England. The Jewett-Eastman House, built around 1850 in Greek Revival style, was the childhood home of writer Sarah Orne Jewett and now serves, per Wikipedia, "as a gallery space and as the visitors center for the adjacent Sarah Orne Jewett House," also under Historic New England's stewardship. The Counting House Museum, operated by the Old Berwick Historical Society, is, per the Society's own site, "open June-Oct on Sundays from 1pm-4pm, and by appointment," with free entry. Vaughan Woods State Park, along the Salmon Falls River on South Berwick's western edge, includes the restored Hamilton House and old-growth forest; per Wikipedia's article on the park, the property "was bequeathed to the state by Elizabeth Vaughan in 1949" and is managed by the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. Hamilton House itself, per Historic New England's own property page, is "a striking Georgian mansion" overlooking the Salmon Falls River and a National Historic Landmark; per Wikipedia's article on the house, it was built between 1787 and 1788.

faq.question: Who runs Powderhouse Hill?
faq.answer: The town of South Berwick owns the hill; the volunteer Powderhouse Hill Ski Club operates the rope tow, and Friends of Powderhouse Hill runs the concession stand, per Seacoastonline's January 29, 2025 report.

faq.question: When does Powderhouse Hill open?
faq.answer: Only when snow allows: per Seacoastonline's report, the hill runs "Wednesday and Friday evenings as well as Saturday and Sunday afternoons" in a given season, and the club has described weighing marginal early-season snow against not skiing at all.

places.name: Vaughan Woods State Park
places.summary: A state park along the Salmon Falls River bequeathed to Maine by Elizabeth Vaughan in 1949, including the restored Hamilton House.
places.history: Per Wikipedia's "Vaughan Woods State Park" article, the park lies along the Salmon Falls River on South Berwick's western edge at the New Hampshire border, including the restored Hamilton House and stands of old-growth forest. The property "was bequeathed to the state by Elizabeth Vaughan in 1949" and is managed by the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry.

places.name: Hamilton House
places.summary: A Georgian mansion overlooking the Salmon Falls River, built in 1787-88 and stewarded by Historic New England as a National Historic Landmark.
places.history: Per Historic New England's own property page, Hamilton House sits "in a picturesque setting overlooking the Salmon Falls River," a "striking Georgian mansion" and National Historic Landmark. Per Wikipedia's article on the house, it was built between 1787 and 1788.
